cases.title: Vinh Loc B Resettlement Quarter, Ho Chi Minh City
cases.place: Vinh Loc B, Binh Chanh district, Ho Chi Minh City, Viet Nam
cases.point: Approximate. The coordinates are the Vinh Loc B resettlement quarter in Binh Chanh district, on the western edge of Ho Chi Minh City, which the project built to rehouse households it displaced. The canal and street works that displaced them lie in the inner city to the east.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit C3887-VN of SDR 148.8 million (about US$222.5 million) for the Vietnam Urban Upgrading Project, approved 29 April 2004, effective 6 October 2004. Additional financing Credit 4604-VN of US$160 million was approved in September 2009, most of it for the Tan Hoa-Lo Gom canal works in Ho Chi Minh City. The project closed on 31 December 2014, two years later than planned. A Japanese PHRD grant (TF-53182) of US$4.839 million was also used. Compensation and resettlement cost US$188.5 million against US$111.3 million estimated at appraisal.

lenders.name: Agence Française de Développement
lenders.role: Expected at appraisal to lend about US$37.5 million towards the Tan Hoa-Lo Gom canal basin works. The World Bank's completion report says that in 2005 it became clear AFD could not provide the money, and the gap was covered by the Bank's additional financing instead.

cases.conditions: The project's resettlement plans required that everyone adversely affected, people without land papers included, be paid for their losses at replacement cost and be helped to keep the living standards and earning capacity they had before construction started (World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, 2015).
cases.community: The project upgraded low-income areas in Ho Chi Minh City, Hai Phong, Nam Dinh and Can Tho. Its largest single work was the Tan Hoa-Lo Gom canal in Ho Chi Minh City, which runs through a densely built part of the city. The World Bank's completion report records 2,917 households permanently relocated and 18,959 households partly affected, against 4,859 and 16,569 estimated at appraisal. For Ho Chi Minh City the resettlement site was Vinh Loc B in Binh Chanh district, given as 30.6 hectares in the completion report's table of resettlement areas, where the project built 529 land plots and 1,939 apartments. Across the four cities the project built 2,641 plots and 2,383 apartments, of which 2,547 plots and apartments were used for resettlement under the project.
cases.outcome:
The Bank's completion report rates compliance with all four safeguard policies satisfactory, and says independent resettlement monitoring consultants confirmed that most affected households were able to maintain or improve their pre-project living standards. The same report records significant delays in organising resettlement and compensation payments, and gives three reasons: verifying the legal status of eligible households took longer than expected, many households only wanted to resettle or receive compensation on days considered auspicious, and government cost norms were often outdated so compensation payments had to be adjusted repeatedly for changes in land prices. The Independent Evaluation Group's 2016 review states that resettlement and compensation to households suffered severe delays, and that delays in counterpart funds for land acquisition and compensation payments led to resettlement taking more time than anticipated. Of 571 complaints collected by the project's grievance system, 568 were resolved at closing; three in Nam Dinh were outstanding and were transferred to projects financed by the city's own funds. Compensation and resettlement cost US$188.5 million against US$111.3 million estimated at appraisal.

Ten years after the loan closed, two Vietnamese outlets reported on the quarter. VietNamNet reported on 26 June 2024 that Vinh Loc B has 2,000 apartments and 529 land plots on 30 hectares, was put into operation in 2013, still has 1,500 apartments unoccupied, and is about 20 km from the city's central area. It quoted a resident, Tran Thi Hong, whose family of four gave up land for the Tham Luong-Ben Cat-Nuoc Len canal improvement project, a different scheme, and moved into a 50 square metre apartment at Vinh Loc B in 2016: she had earned VND 12 million a month selling bread and said her income has dropped by half; where she was housed there were 60 apartments but only 10 households when she arrived, and some households left after several months because they could not find jobs. A second resident, Nguyen Thi Hoa, who moved in during 2018, said the area painted white has become grey because of mould and that the walls inside apartments are cracked. VnExpress reported on 6 June 2024 that Vinh Loc B has 1,900 apartments, 80 percent of them unoccupied, and that of the vacant resettlement units counted by the Department of Construction nearly 9,000 are in Ho Chi Minh City, of which Vinh Loc B accounts for nearly a quarter. It quoted Tran Huu Son, 56, of District 6, whose family handed over their land to the state in 2012 for the Tan Hoa-Lo Gom canal sanitation project, the work this loan financed: he was offered either cash or an apartment at Vinh Loc B 12 km from his old house and took the cash, which was not enough to buy a new apartment, because the resettlement area was too far away and would affect the family's livelihood.

cases.displaced_label: 2,917 households permanently relocated, 18,959 partly affected (World Bank)
cases.displaced_note: The World Bank's completion report gives 2,917 households permanently relocated and 18,959 households partly affected at closing, against appraisal estimates of 4,859 and 16,569. It does not convert these into numbers of people. ICIJ's 2015 harvest of World Bank documents lists 57,047 people for this project; ICIJ says it searched the documents for the terms "affected", "PAP" or "displaced", used the average number of family members per household where only households were counted, and because not all documents distinguish temporary from permanent impacts "decided to include all impacts".
cases.confidence_note: The displacement figures and the delays in paying compensation come from the World Bank's own completion report and from the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it. The Evaluation Group is the Bank's own evaluation arm and is not independent of the lender. The condition of the Vinh Loc B quarter and the residents' accounts come from two Vietnamese outlets reporting in June 2024. Three counts of the apartments at Vinh Loc B differ and each is given here as its source published it: the completion report's table of resettlement areas gives 1,939, VietNamNet gives 2,000 and VnExpress gives 1,900. The two outlets' vacancy figures, 1,500 apartments unoccupied and 80 percent unoccupied, are of the same order and are not a disagreement. Their distance figures measure different things: VietNamNet gives about 20 km from the city's central area, VnExpress gives 12 km between one resident's former home and the apartment he was offered. Of the two residents quoted on conditions at the quarter, Tran Huu Son lost land to the canal this loan financed; Tran Thi Hong lost land to a different canal project and was housed at the same site. No Inspection Panel complaint was filed on this project.
cases.ecosystem: The Tan Hoa-Lo Gom canal was dredged and embanked; the completion report says the main environmental risk was handling and disposing of over 90,000 cubic metres of dredged material, and that chemical oxygen demand in the canal fell from 811 mg/l in 2009 to 80-130 mg/l in 2015.

lvwhy.project: An IDA-financed urban works project paid for the canal, street and drainage works that required the clearance, and for the resettlement housing.
lvwhy.land: Land in four cities was acquired from 21,876 households, 2,917 of them losing their homes.

cases.whole: The Vietnam Urban Upgrading Project, approved in April 2004 and closed at the end of 2014, financed drainage, roads, water and sanitation in low-income areas of Ho Chi Minh City, Hai Phong, Nam Dinh and Can Tho, together with land titling, a housing loan programme and resettlement housing. Its largest single work was the rehabilitation of the Tan Hoa-Lo Gom canal in Ho Chi Minh City. Total project cost was US$509.3 million against US$417.5 million at appraisal.

cases.title: Urban Water and Wastewater Project: Structures Paid at Part of Replacement Value
cases.place: Ninh Binh city, Ninh Binh province, and Thai Hoa, Nghe An province, Viet Nam
cases.point: Approximate. The coordinates are Ninh Binh city, one of the two towns where the World Bank's completion report says the compensation gaps were not confirmed as settled; the other is Thai Hoa in Nghe An, about 120 km to the south-west. The project worked in 11 towns in 10 provinces.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA and IBRD)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-49480 of US$200 million for the Urban Water Supply and Wastewater Project, approved 24 May 2011, effective 7 October 2011, closed 31 December 2019. Additional financing of US$69 million (IBRD-86210) and US$50 million (IDA-58170) was added in May 2016 for a wastewater and drainage subproject in Di An. Total Bank financing disbursed was US$266.5 million of a US$299.6 million project.

cases.conditions: A resettlement policy framework and 15 resettlement action plans were prepared and disclosed in December 2010 under the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12. The Bank's completion report states that compensation levels and assistance were to be set at replacement cost and to account for living standards and earning capacity before the project (World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, 2020).
cases.community: The project built water supply, wastewater and drainage works in Di An and My Phuoc (Binh Duong), Dong Xoai (Binh Phuoc), Phu Quoc (Kien Giang), Da Lat (Lam Dong), Thai Hoa (Nghe An), Ninh Binh, Tam Ky (Quang Nam), Uong Bi (Quang Ninh), Dong Ha (Quang Tri) and Bim Son (Thanh Hoa). Di An was added with the additional financing in 2016. At appraisal 870,583 square metres of land were to be acquired and 556 households affected, 9 of them relocated, and three household businesses were expected to be affected. For the additional financing a further 69,732 square metres were required for the wastewater treatment plant and pumping stations, permanently affecting 57 households, three firms and five organisations. During implementation 3,081 households were affected: 45 had to be relocated, 455 lost more than 20 percent of their agricultural land, and 2,581 were marginally affected through partial losses of agricultural or residential land, of secondary structures, or for temporary periods during construction.
cases.outcome: The Bank's completion report says all compensation to households was completed and that at project closure there were no grievances or outstanding issues, and that monitoring surveys by an independent resettlement monitoring consultant confirmed that most affected households were able to maintain or improve their pre-project living standards. In the same passage it records that local authorities often applied government policies where gaps were identified in compensation plans, "including assistance to households that lost 30 percent of agricultural land, and compensation for structures on agricultural land from 50 percent to 80 percent of its replacement value". The provincial project management units and local authorities were requested to solve those issues during implementation. The report then states that by the end of the project "such issues were addressed in most subprojects, except in Thai Hoa and Ninh Binh subprojects where the status has not been affirmed officially to the World Bank". The report also records that documentation of land acquisition was not adequately prepared in some subprojects, and that in Di An the preparation of a cadastral map and identification of landowners took more than one year.

cases.displaced_label: 3,081 affected households, 45 moved, 455 lost more than 20 percent of their farmland (World Bank)
cases.displaced_note: The World Bank's completion report gives 3,081 affected households during implementation, of which 45 were relocated, 455 lost more than 20 percent of their agricultural land and 2,581 were marginally affected. ICIJ's 2015 harvest of World Bank documents lists 16,983 people for this project; ICIJ says it searched the documents for the terms "affected", "PAP" or "displaced", used the average number of family members per household where only households were counted, and because not all documents distinguish temporary from permanent impacts "decided to include all impacts". The project was still running when ICIJ's data was compiled in 2014.
cases.confidence_note: The World Bank's own completion report is the only source found for this case, and it says two things that pull against each other: that all compensation was completed with no outstanding issues at closure, and that compensation for structures on agricultural land was applied at 50 to 80 percent of replacement value and that the status of this had not been affirmed officially to the Bank in the Thai Hoa and Ninh Binh subprojects. The report does not say how many households in those two towns were affected by the shortfall, or when or whether it was made good. No independent documentation was found. Independent documentation of resettlement in Viet Nam is thin and the lender's own record is often all there is.

cases.title: Bac Son-Nam Hai Road, Haiphong: Resettlement Held Up for Years
cases.place: Bac Son to Nam Hai east-west road link, Haiphong, Viet Nam
cases.point: Approximate. The coordinates are the midpoint of the Bac Son-Nam Hai east-west road link, which runs across Haiphong from Bac Son in An Duong to Nam Hai in Hai An.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-49000 of US$175 million for the Haiphong Urban Transport Project, approved 29 March 2011, effective 28 July 2011, closed 29 February 2020 after the closing date was moved three years and two months from 31 December 2016. US$152.5 million was disbursed. The Haiphong city government was to put in US$101.61 million, including compensation, resettlement and livelihood restoration for affected people and the building of resettlement sites.

cases.conditions: The project's resettlement policy framework, prepared under the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12, was approved by the prime minister's office; two resettlement action plans were agreed with the Bank and approved by the Haiphong City People's Committee (World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, 2020).
cases.community: The resettlement policy framework was prepared for an initial survey of 3,037 project-affected households in 13 communes and wards of Haiphong, in five districts, which the completion report also gives as 12,605 persons. It identified 909 households that had to be relocated. Acquiring the land to develop the resettlement sites affected a further 871 households, 4,223 persons; the report says those households were affected by that acquisition and does not say how many of them were moved.
cases.outcome: The Bank's completion report says delayed and difficult execution of resettlement and land acquisition led to slower implementation progress, and names the cause: "the Haiphong Government's financial constraints in providing counterpart funding and delayed hand-over of the accessible sites to the contractors". At the mid-term review on 6 October 2014 the Bank identified inadequate counterpart funding as a cause for delays; that situation delayed construction progress for nearly eight months, and the project was restructured to reallocate savings to three resettlement site contracts. Delays continued through the last three years of the project, which the report attributes to persisting difficulties in resettlement processes and insufficient budget allocation in the city's Medium-Term Investment Plan for 2016 to 2020. By November 2018, less than 18 months before closure, there were 69 outstanding resettlement cases, nearly 6 percent of the 3,037 total. Completion of the road component accumulated nearly 3.5 years in delays, of which the report says more than 80 percent is attributable to resolving that remaining 6 percent of cases. Implementation progress was rated moderately unsatisfactory in six of the 19 progress reports listed in the completion report. By October 2019, 109 outstanding resettlement cases, 3.5 percent of cases, had been resolved, with three outstanding at that time; one remained outstanding at project closure and is reported as resolved as of 1 October 2020. The road opening ceremony took place on 3 May 2020.

cases.title: Mekong Delta Transport Project: Compensation Unfinished at Closing
cases.place: Mekong Delta waterway and road corridors, 13 provinces and Ho Chi Minh City, Viet Nam
cases.point: Approximate. The coordinates are Binh Thuy district, Can Tho, where the project widened National Highway 91 between km 7 and km 14 and the completion report's annex records 833,141 square metres of land and 508 affected households. The project's works ran through 13 provinces and Ho Chi Minh City.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-4306 of SDR 137.20 million (US$207.7 million equivalent) for the Mekong Delta Transport Infrastructure Development Project, approved 22 May 2007, effective 14 April 2008. Additional financing (IDA-5200) raised the credits to SDR 238.5 million (US$363.7 million equivalent), of which US$7.42 million was cancelled. Closing moved from 30 December 2013 to 30 June 2016. Resettlement and rehabilitation of affected people, US$130.98 million, was financed entirely by the government.

lenders.name: Government of Australia (AusAID, later DFAT)
lenders.role: Trust fund grants TF-91332 and TF-13700 of AU$47.4 million (US$40 million equivalent).

cases.conditions: A resettlement policy framework complying with the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12 was prepared by the government and cleared by the Bank before appraisal, and applied to every subproject for the life of the project; sub-project resettlement plans had to be cleared by the Bank before works began (World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, 2017).
cases.community: The project was implemented by Viet Nam's Ministry of Transport. Two first-phase resettlement plans counted 7,245 displaced persons on the waterways and 2,840 on the national highways and provincial roads. By the end of the project the number of affected households had risen from 15,000 to 22,663, an increase of over 30 percent, on 518.43 hectares of land. The completion report says the majority of those affected were only marginally affected, losing trees, garden fences and similar. Its annex lists the households by component and province: 3,638 on the national highways component in Tra Vinh and Can Tho; 7,620 on the waterway component in An Giang, Dong Thap, Kien Giang, Tien Giang, Soc Trang, Bac Lieu, Long An and Ho Chi Minh City; and 11,405 on the provincial roads component in An Giang, Soc Trang, Ca Mau, Bac Lieu, Tra Vinh, Long An, Tien Giang, Ben Tre, Vinh Long, Can Tho, Hau Giang, Dong Thap and Kien Giang.
cases.outcome: The Bank's completion report says there was general compliance with the principles of the resettlement policy framework throughout the life of the project, and that "in the initial years, there were a small number of instances identified where affected persons were not compensated in accordance with the approved safeguards measures", which the implementing units addressed. At the closing date of 30 June 2016, compensation was not completed for about 110 households under the waterway component because of a compensation rate issue. The government committed to continue with the compensation until completion under the project's resettlement policy framework and under monthly Bank monitoring; when the report was written in early 2017, 30 households still remained, with compensation planned to complete by the end of March 2017. The report also records that insufficient allocation of counterpart funds for resettlement compensation presented a critical barrier to progress throughout implementation: contractors were not always able to access construction sites because of unresolved resettlement claims, especially on the national waterway component; provincial authorities advanced their state budget for immediate compensation and were reimbursed later; delays in resettlement progress increased compensation payments over the course of the project; and the need for an unforeseen increase of US$52 million in counterpart funds was flagged in late 2015 to cover additional resettlement costs.

cases.title: Coastal Cities Sanitation Project: Quy Nhon, Nha Trang and Dong Hoi
cases.place: Quy Nhon, Binh Dinh province, Viet Nam, with works also in Nha Trang and Dong Hoi
cases.point: Approximate. The coordinates are Quy Nhon, where the 11 households whose compensation was still being settled at closure lived and where the project built one resettlement site. The project also worked in Nha Trang, about 170 km south, and Dong Hoi, about 500 km north.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-42530 and IDA-48850 totalling US$190.243 million for the Coastal Cities Environmental Sanitation Project, approved 19 December 2006, effective 15 June 2007, closed 30 November 2014; US$185.53 million was disbursed.

lenders.name: Government of Japan (PHRD grant)
lenders.role: Policy and Human Resources Development Fund grant TF056325 of US$4.616 million, of which US$4.2 million was disbursed.

lenders.name: Global Environment Facility
lenders.role: GEF grant TF094335 of US$5 million for the associated VN-GEF Coastal Cities Project, approved 23 June 2009, closed 31 December 2014; US$4.3 million was disbursed.

cases.conditions: A resettlement policy framework was prepared under the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12, and ten resettlement action plans were prepared under it for the three cities. One of the project's own indicators was the share of affected households that had received compensation as set out in their resettlement action plan before their assets were taken from them, along with relocation, transition and subsistence allowances, and incomes restored to pre-project levels (World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, 2015).
cases.community: The project built sewers, wastewater treatment plants, drainage, flood protection, solid waste works and school toilets in Dong Hoi, Quy Nhon and Nha Trang. It acquired about 189.4 hectares in the three cities from 1,247 affected households, of which 223 had to be resettled, against 245 in the approved resettlement plans. A total of 259 land plots on five resettlement sites were provided; one site in Quy Nhon was built by the project.
cases.outcome: The Bank's completion report says VND 233 billion, about US$11.1 million, was paid to the affected people, and rates resettlement moderately satisfactory, with the independent resettlement monitoring consultant reporting that all the surveyed relocated project-affected people were able to restore or improve their lost assets and livelihood. The same report records that the project received complaints in 2014 from 11 households in Quy Nhon City related to their compensation and resettlement, before project closure. VND 3 billion, about US$0.14 million, was transferred to state treasury accounts for those 11 households, and the compensation plan was endorsed by the Binh Dinh Provincial People's Committee; the report bases this on the last report submitted by the Quy Nhon subproject at the end of March 2015, and does not say whether the households took the money. A resettlement site was also developed by the project in Nha Trang to satisfy requests from affected people to be relocated in the vicinity, but the city allocated existing available sites to them instead.

cases.title: Mekong Delta Water Management Project: 260 Resettlement Grievances
cases.place: Seven Mekong Delta provinces, Viet Nam; coordinates at Bac Lieu city
cases.point: Approximate. The coordinates are Bac Lieu city. Bac Lieu is one of the seven provinces covered, and the Bank's completion report names Bac Lieu subprojects among the works, including the Dong Nang Ren and Phuoc Long schemes and the construction of 14 bridges. The project's works were spread across all seven provinces.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-49510 of US$160 million for the Mekong Delta Water Management for Rural Development Project, approved 7 June 2011, effective 7 October 2011, closed 15 September 2017 after an extension from 31 March 2017. US$134.3 million was disbursed. The government was to put in US$46.6 million, of which US$45.1 million was provided.

cases.conditions: A resettlement policy framework and resettlement action plans were prepared and accepted by the Bank under its involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12, and resettlement plans had to be in place before civil works began on each subproject (World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, 2018).
cases.community: The project was implemented by Viet Nam's Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development. It built irrigation, drainage and salinity-control works, rural water supply and bridges in the western Mekong Delta. The appraisal document names the target area as An Giang, Ca Mau, Hau Giang, Soc Trang, Bac Lieu and Kien Giang provinces and the municipality of Can Tho, which it calls the seven provinces; the completion report names six of them. The Bank's completion report records 5,435 households affected by the project: 215 had to be relocated, 304 lost part of their agricultural land and 70 had to rebuild their house on their remaining land.
cases.outcome: The Bank's completion report says the project faced a significant number of issues related to resettlement, and lists the causes: disputes over land title, rates of compensation, differences between the resettlement policies of the Vietnamese government and the Bank, and the delay of the payment of resettlement compensations due to lack of counterpart funding. It says this resulted in some delays in project implementation. There were 260 resettlement-related grievances, 250 of which could be solved by the provincial project management units themselves. The report says that at project completion all grievances and outstanding issues were solved by local authorities and the project management units, that all adversely affected persons including informal settlers were financially compensated at replacement costs and supported to maintain their living standards and income-earning capacities, and that monitoring surveys by independent resettlement monitoring consultants confirmed that affected households were able to maintain or improve their pre-project living standards. The Independent Evaluation Group's 2018 review of the report states that the resettlement policy framework and resettlement action plans were prepared and found acceptable by the Bank and gives no figures of its own.

sources.title: Implementation Completion and Results Report: VN - Mekong Delta Water Management for Rural Dev (P113949)
ICR Review: VN-Mekong Delta Water Mgmt for Rural Dev (P113949)
Data dive: how to mine World Bank resettlement documents

cases.displaced_label: 5,435 affected households, 215 moved, 304 lost part of their farmland, 70 rebuilt on remaining land (World Bank)
cases.displaced_note: The World Bank's completion report gives 5,435 affected households, of which 215 were relocated, 304 lost part of their agricultural land and 70 had to rebuild a house on their remaining land. ICIJ's 2015 harvest of World Bank documents lists 15,504 people for this project; ICIJ says it searched the documents for the terms "affected", "PAP" or "displaced", used the average number of family members per household where only households were counted, and because not all documents distinguish temporary from permanent impacts "decided to include all impacts". The project was still running when ICIJ's data was compiled in 2014.
cases.confidence_note: The World Bank's own completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it are the only sources found for this case. The report records the 260 grievances and the delay in paying resettlement compensation caused by the lack of counterpart funding, and also states that everything was settled by completion and that people were compensated at replacement costs. The report does not say how long the payments were late, how many households were affected by the delay, or what the grievances asked for, and no independent documentation was found. Independent documentation of resettlement in Viet Nam is thin and the lender's own record is often all there is. This project is a Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development irrigation and water supply loan of 2011 and is separate from the Mekong Delta Transport Infrastructure Development loan of 2007, a Ministry of Transport road and waterway loan in overlapping provinces and years, which is a separate case.
cases.ecosystem: The project built salinity-control and drainage works and ring dykes in the Mekong Delta and ran an integrated pest management programme in all seven provinces to limit the increase in agricultural chemical use it expected from more irrigated land.

lvwhy.project: An IDA credit of US$160 million paid for the irrigation, drainage and water supply works that required the land.
lvwhy.land: Land was taken from 5,435 households across seven provinces, 215 of which had to be relocated.

cases.whole: The Mekong Delta Water Management for Rural Development Project financed irrigation and drainage schemes, salinity control, ring dykes, rural water supply and bridges in seven Mekong Delta provinces between 2011 and 2017. Total project cost was US$179.4 million. The Bank rated the outcome moderately satisfactory and the quality of monitoring modest.

dropped.reason: Dropped: ICIJ's 773,838 is not a count of people moved, and no documented failure was found. Five documents were read in full from disk as text: the Project Appraisal Document of 21 October 2004, the Integrated Safeguards Data Sheet of 24 May 2004, the 2009 additional financing project paper, the 13 December 2014 Implementation Completion and Results Report and the Independent Evaluation Group's 12 May 2015 review of it. The figure 773,838 appears in none of them, and does not appear in the resettlement plan volume headed 'Project Affected Persons', which was also read. The project's document file holds 91 items, including more than 20 provincial resettlement action plans, and those were not all read, so the absence claim covers the five core documents and not the whole file. The ISDS states: 'The Project will not involve any major resettlement but will entail land acquisition and resettlement impacts due to construction of new lines and substations'; 'In the first phase of project 131,955 households will be affected by the Project. The number of DPs is high because of the DPs are scattered along the lines'; 'Most of impacts on land will be temporary'; and 'Impacts on houses will be mostly partial and generally will not require the relocation of families outside their residential plots.' The appraisal document's Annex 13 classifies impacts in seven categories, five of them temporary right-of-way impacts, and its Table 1 for the six Phase 1(a) provinces gives, in a column headed 'Number of Families Losing >10% of Productive Land Holding', a total of 178 families, all of them in Vinh Phuc and none in the other five provinces, against 299,746 square metres of permanent acquisition and 14,256,140 square metres of temporary acquisition; the table carries a note that the numbers could differ from the detailed measurement survey carried out later. The completion report says 'The negative impacts of project activities are generally minor because most of the lines were rehabilitated from the existing ones. A small volume of land acquisition was required for the new alignments and substations', records difficulties including long negotiations with affected households on compensation packages, and rates overall compliance with social safeguard policies satisfactory; the IEG review repeats this. Neither gives any figure for people physically moved. On what ICIJ's figure counts: 773,838 is about 5.9 times the 131,955 households the ISDS says would be affected in the first phase, and ICIJ's method page says it used the average number of family members per household where only households were counted. The project's own provincial resettlement plans, however, report average family sizes of 4.3 to 4.93 persons, which applied to 131,955 households give 567,000 to 651,000, not 773,838. The 131,955 figure is for the first phase only and the project ran in about 25 provinces, so the figure may be a sum across phases. The documents read do not say how ICIJ arrived at it, and no arithmetic reconstruction of it is offered here.

Dropped: a rural distribution project covering about 45 provinces in three power company areas, with no identified community and no number. The 24 December 2013 Implementation Completion and Results Report was read in full from disk as text (3,428 lines). It says the project 'caused modest land acquisition for the individual project affected household and small community-wide socioeconomic impacts', that many subprojects aimed to upgrade systems based on an existing right of way, and that 'The land acquisition and compensation activities by Implementation Agencies satisfactorily complied with OP 4.12, Involuntary Resettlement'. It lists significant land acquisition challenges including 'disagreements by affected households with proposed compensation rates'. One passage is worth recording. In Annex 7, the summary of the borrower's own completion report, Central Power Corporation (formerly Power Company No. 3), which implemented the component covering about 11 provinces in the central region, writes: 'The conduct of compensation and resettlement was difficult, complicated and long-lasted. Compensation unit price in provinces was low as compared with average price of the market, interfering significantly in compensation declaration to local residents. Simultaneously, some problems arose such as people did not accept compensation, obstructed construction and made long solving time.' That is the implementing company's own account of its own work. It names no province, no commune and no number of households, gives no date, and records no outcome for any identified person, so it cannot carry a case or fix a point on a map.

Dropped: the recorded displacement was small and no failure is documented. Two documents were read in full from disk as text: the Independent Evaluation Group's 9 December 2013 ICR Review and its 20 August 2019 Project Performance Assessment Report, which is based on a field mission. The assessment report says: 'In all, 5,974 households were negatively affected; of these 167 households were classified as "severely affected" with loses of more than 20 percent of their land. Sixty-five households required resettlement.' Sixty-nine households of the Tay and Nung minorities were affected at the Cau Son-Cam Son irrigation scheme and an ethnic minority development plan was prepared and implemented for them. The report says overall environmental and social safeguards compliance was adequate. The 2013 review says a review of technical design 'was able to reduce the number of affected households from the initial 11,000 to about 6,000, although the ICR does not evaluate the adequacy of the compensation'; that absence of evaluation is not a finding of harm. ICIJ's 53,600 is of the same order as that initial estimate of 11,000 households rather than as what the field-based evaluation records happened.

Dropped: no identified community, no number and no documented failure. Two documents were read in full from disk as text: the 31 December 2014 Implementation Completion and Results Report (2,395 lines) and the Independent Evaluation Group's 26 May 2015 review of it (503 lines). The completion report says involuntary resettlement on the transmission investments, especially the 220 kV to 500 kV subprojects, was challenging, that the magnitude of impacts there is more significant than for lower voltage investments including 'more severe impacts, including physical relocation', and that implementing agencies 'faced a lot of difficulties in: (i) negotiating with affected households about compensation packages'. It then states that 'IAs adequately managed activities related to involuntary resettlement' and that 'The overall compliance with the triggered social safeguard policies is "Satisfactory"'. Neither document gives any number of people or households affected or physically moved, names an affected community, or records a compensation failure.

Dropped: the Bank's own completion report shows the figure is not a count of people moved. The 14 June 2019 Implementation Completion and Results Report was read in full from disk as text. It states: 'The PCs were able to minimize physical relocation (only five households were relocated out of 12,880 Project Affected Households) by the construction/execution of 169 subprojects', and that 'Although the number of affected households was high (owing to the inherent nature of linear projects), the impact at household level was low and/manageable.' Compensation paid to affected households totalled VND 287 billion, about US$12.4 million. As of 31 May 2019 the social safeguard instruments had been completed in 167 of 169 subprojects, with two pending. Safeguards were rated satisfactory at closing. Against five households relocated, ICIJ's 31,581 is a project-affected-persons figure in the widest sense, and no documented failure was found.
